title: Electronic instruments and the voice
summary: Maxwell dislikes synthesizers and electric sound.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: Talking about all the electronic business in music, the recording part of the electronic part of the music is what bothers me the least of it. What bothers me the most is the electronic instruments that are coming up, the electric pianoes, the Moog and the synthesizers and everything.

And I know that these young guys playing them are dedicated musicians, I know they get glassy-eyed when they talk about it and they study hard and they work hard. But I really don't much like the sound of those things. And this music called fusion music, WRVR, Jazz never sounded better, you know, and that's all they're playing, these things that it sounds like one stage more will be to the computer. You know, they're playing these mathematically (Humming), pentatonic scales and these worked out mathematical-------, because they're playing at speeds that I know is not improvised, it's worked out, it's so complicated.
And it really bothers me because my own feeling is, I never even liked the electric guitar.

I stopped right there. I didn't even like that. Now you go up to these amplified instruments, I don't like them. I just don't like them. I don't object to them, I can give you philosophical reasons why I don't like them; but I just don't like them. I start from emotion. I don't like them. They sound fake to me, they bother me, they just sound ugly.
You can never get the natural sound out of them.

Well, there is no natural sound. It's an electronic sound. Music, the greatest music in the world is the voice. That's the original music, I think, the voice and the heartbeat is the drum. And then through the voice you came to the trumpet or the horn, whatever. And everything is an imitation of the voice and the heartbeat. And as long as you're blowing your breath into the instrument or you're plucking on the string of an instrument, you could control the feeling of it. You know, you could put the expression -- well, you know how you feel when you play sometimes, your heart beats faster, you feel your face flush, and you'll start to play things you'd never think of. And this excitement generates more excitement that makes you play better.

And when you play an electronic instrument, you're at the mercy of the electrons. You don't even have pedals to change the volume, let alone the quality of the tone. There is no tone, you know. I guess in your case, you would press the bow down, you would pluck it in a different way. In my case I would choke the tone with my lips or increase the volume or something. You don't do these things consciously but as your feelings increase, your sound changes. And you can't do that electronically. Or if you can, it's too subtle for me to hear.

You have no control of your own power there, because as you say, now you can hear a flute in the middle of a brass package. I know in the case of a bass, I mean the biggest control of an artist in his music is to be able to control it and make his own dynamics.

Here, I can take a bass fiddle, I get this godawful sound coming through an amplifier, and all I can do is make it louder or softer. I can blow the whole band down, but the pitching, the quality, you just can't duplicate it.
And you're one of the few hold-outs that are still playing acoustic bass. And it's such a thrill to hear it, it's such a warm sound. And you've always got a beautiful sound anyhow.
But it's kind of hard to fight with it all the time.

I know it. And I guess from traveling on the planes like you do, it must be an awful temptation to just slip a fender bass, a chunk of wood with a microphone on it, and ship it through, you know. So if they splinter it, it isn't going to make any difference.
I think that's what would make me go into retirement quicker than anything else, Jimmy.

Well, I think if I had to put one of those microphones in my mouthpiece, play that way, I would give up. It's the same thing because, you know, they've got dials that can make your tone an octave lower or you can get an octave higher at the same time, or you can get a buzz in it. Miles Davis fooled around with one of those for a while.
